summary: Which law applies depends on religion and community. Under the Civil Code, children and parents have a protected share; Muslims follow Islamic fixed shares and can will at most one third. A foreigner's movables follow their national law but a foreigner cannot hold Indonesian freehold land, and Indonesia has no trust law and has not joined the Hague Trusts Convention.
reserved_share: Civil Code (non-Muslims): children, legitime portie of one half of their intestate share with one child, two thirds with two, three quarters with three or more (art. 914); parents one half (art. 915). Muslims: Compilation of Islamic Law (Inpres 1/1991) fixed shares, with bequests limited to one third (art. 195).
foreign_law_note: The Algemene Bepalingen (AB) arts. 16-17 apply personal-status law by nationality to foreigners and the law of the place for immovables, so a foreigner's movables follow their national law. Foreigners cannot own land (hak milik) under the Agrarian Law and Indonesian courts may apply public policy. Customary (adat) law also applies to some groups.
trust_note: Not on the HCCH status table. Indonesia has no trust law; Law 42/1999 covers only fiduciary security. Foreign trusts are not clearly recognised and there is no special trust tax regime. Foundations (yayasan) are under Law 16/2001 as amended by Law 28/2004; they must pursue social, religious or humanitarian aims, and founders cannot take profit.
open_questions: Confirm Civil Code arts. 913-915 fractions from the official text; I used the standard legitime portie figures and the source retrieved did not quote them.
